title: Karkain native compilation path -- qualified feature matrix
scope: The Karkain-owned native path (kcc), i.e. `karkain build --target native-x86_64-<os>` with NO C compiler and NO Go toolchain in the program-compilation path. This is the v1.2.0 'Sovereignty I' qualification surface. It is NOT the C-backend path and NOT the WASM path.

statuses.supported: Lowered by the self-hosted driver, with a passing gate that executes or byte-compares it.
statuses.implemented_not_gated: Lowered by the driver, but no gate exercises the kcc side of it yet. Not advertised as supported.
statuses.not_supported: Refused BY NAME with a diagnostic and no image. Never silently mis-lowered.
statuses.blocked: Blocked by a known architectural dependency outside this path.

features.construct: call to a user function with arguments
return value from a user function
array element read with a VARIABLE index
string byte index (`s[i]`) as a one-byte view
array element read with an ARITHMETIC index
array iteration in a C-style `for` loop
array element inside an arithmetic expression
array element passed to a function
nested array access (an index that is itself an element read)

features.note: A runtime error with a non-zero exit and no value printed. The diagnostic text goes to stderr, which the Phase-152-B0 GetStdHandle limitation leaves empty on this host, so the exit status is the observable.

features.construct: array index that is not an integer expression
array element of a non-int type
features.note: Array elements are int literals only.

features.construct: sha256_hex builtin (64 lowercase hex digits, strlen-truncated)
features.note: Executed PE exact-byte goldens, C-backend and Go-native behavioral differentials, FIPS-derived K/IV constants present in the image, refusal rows, determinism. Byte-identity with the Go native helper is not claimed: kcc uses a frame-resident K table and true 32-bit ALU forms.

features.construct: `push(array, value)` through the native CLI target
features.note: The driver's push() emission has a pre-existing bad rodata patch position; the PE patch guard now refuses it with `native pe: rodata patch ... does not fit the section body`. The former execution gate was corrected to pin the refusal rather than papering over it. This is not fixed by the for-in slice. The same refusal is also pinned by TestPhase151A9I_RefusalsAreByName in pkg/cli/phase151a9i_forin_test.go.

features.construct: the reporter's read-only data is interned in the oracle's order, at the interned OFFSETS
features.note: The driver used to append the reporter's four strings AFTER the program's own literals (the oracle interns them first, because the reporter helper is emitted before the user function) and to bake the LIST POSITION of the array-bounds call site's two strings where the interned OFFSET belongs -- so the diagnostic pointed at the wrong bytes. Both are corrected, and the array-index shape is now byte-identical to the oracle's. The gate reads the section's entries out of each image, in order, with their offsets.

features.construct: native frame layout (the frame-size immediate) matches the Go oracle's
features.note: The frame-size immediate is read out of each generated image and compared with the oracle's, for both targets. The Linux target matters because the Windows 16-byte rounding quantises an 8-byte difference away.

features.construct: the map-stage frame unit is reserved program-wide
native register allocation (int locals into callee-saved registers)
features.note: Opt-in: the switch is KARKAIN_NATIVE_REGALLOC=1 and the DEFAULT is the stack-based path, which is the qualified implementation. The allocator engages only under pressure (control flow and at least five simultaneously-live int locals), promotes int locals into R12-R15, and never splits a live range -- a candidate that cannot get a register keeps its frame slot, so the frame does not shrink.
The driver lowers maps (natMapFind/natMapSet/natMapGet) and the Go oracle gates them in pkg/native/phase150b3c_test.go, but no gate exercises the kcc side of the map path yet.

v1.2.7 (NAT-STREQ). Exact-byte executed PE goldens on Windows, byte-identical Linux ELF against the Go oracle, and refusal rows for non-equality kinds. Equality over strings compares content (length first, then bytes), not pointers. The string staging area is reserved program-wide, including inside `if`/`while`/`for` bodies, so a loop's index slot is not clobbered.

v1.2.7 (NAT-STRSLICE). View form (no allocation): result is (s.ptr + a, b - a) with bounds 0 <= a <= b <= len, loud Int3 on violation. Present bounds are integer expressions, not only literals. An absent bound is an EMPTY node and the emitter substitutes 0 / len(s).
v1.2.7 drew the boundary deliberately: `==`/`!=` compare content, ordering has no defined semantics in this value model and is refused by name (`string ordering ('<') is not supported`).
The rodata cursor for the bounds check is threaded per statement list in this driver.

features.construct: string binding inside a loop body
features.note: The rodata cursor is threaded per statement list in this driver.
The arena is sized at compile time on the assumption that each allocation site runs at most once.
Same arena bound as the row above.

features.construct: `for ... in` iteration over an array variable
features.note: Exact-byte executed PE goldens on Windows, byte-identical Linux ELF against the Go oracle everywhere, nested loops, break/continue, an index inside the body, and the hidden-index frame slot. A literal iterator (`for x in [1, 2]`) remains refused by both engines.
The subset has no `if`, so a recursive function cannot terminate: both engines stack-overflow identically. Parity, not support.
The native path has no stdlib runtime: `import std.*` is refused by the driver. This is closure condition 2 of v1.2.0, carried to v1.3.0 as UNMET.
Closure condition 3 of v1.2.0, carried to v1.3.0 as UNMET.

v1.2.17 platform decision: C23-only (WinHTTP/Schannel on Windows, OpenSSL on POSIX). The native runtime has no socket syscalls, so TLS cannot be layered there; the gate asserts the C23 path on both engines.

v1.2.18 platform decision: C23-only. The native runtime has no socket syscalls or concurrency scheduler; a silent first client proves the C23 path dispatches per-connection spawned workers on both engines.

v1.2.19 platform decision: C23-only. The native runtime has no OS process/metric syscalls; the gate proves real PID/CPU/memory/uptime values and a self-containing process list on both engines and pins native refusal by name.
v1.2.20 platform decision: C23-only. The native driver has no JSON builtins and refuses json_* by name; the gate proves nested parse/query/serialize and deterministic errors on both engines.
v1.2.21 platform decision: C23-only. The native runtime has no UDP sockets; the gate proves a Karkain-bound UDP socket sends and receives a real datagram on both engines.
v1.2.21 platform decision: C23-only. The native runtime has no TCP socket reuse for RFC 6455 frames; the gate proves handshake and masked text frames over loopback on both engines.

v1.2.22 platform decision: C23-only. The native runtime has no FFI, sqlite3 linkage or malloc-based DB runtime; the gate proves in-memory and temp-file SQLite with deterministic errors on both engines.
v1.2.13 platform decision: native runtime has no atomic primitives (no lock prefix / fence emission). C23 path keeps full `@atomic_*` surface via C11 stdatomic.
The native path has no concurrency runtime.

independence_evidence.claim: The qualified native path does not invoke a C compiler, a C source generator, the Go compiler or the Go runtime.
independence_evidence.how: pkg/cli/phase151h_qualification_test.go installs PATH shims for `gcc` and `go` that log every invocation, warms the self-hosted compiler OUTSIDE the trace, and then builds a program natively with the shims on PATH. An empty log is the evidence.

known_limitations: The self-hosted driver has no register allocator, so a function with five or more simultaneously-live int locals AND control flow is encoded differently from the Go oracle (which has the Phase-150C allocator). The difference is an encoding strategy, not a wrong answer; the boundary is pinned by TestPhaseNATIf_TheRegisterAllocatorBoundaryIsPinned.
The rodata cursor is threaded per statement list in the driver, so a STRING literal inside a branch or a loop body is refused. An integer binding inside a branch or a loop body is supported.

A program with an array IS byte-identical to the Go oracle: the TWO bytes that used to differ -- the absolute rodata addresses of the runtime-error reporter's strings -- were closed by NAT-RODATA, and the cause was not an interning ORDER difference (the two engines' read-only sections were byte-identical) but a reference-resolution defect: the driver baked the LIST POSITION of the array-bounds call site's two strings where the interned OFFSET belongs, so it pointed at the middle of "runtime error: " instead of at the message and the file name. The FRAME matched the oracle exactly before that too -- the 8-byte difference NAT-FRAME closed was an unreserved map-stage slot, not a rounding rule.

ONE rodata difference remains, and it is a LAYOUT difference with no correctness consequence: the oracle interns the array-bounds call site's two strings AT THE FIRST INDEX SITE, so a program that binds a string literal AFTER an index site puts them earlier, while the driver groups them after the literals. Measured: 39 differing bytes for such a program; the diagnostic's text is identical in both engines. Closing it would mean re-deriving the interning order from the emitter's walk, or interning at emission time as the oracle does. Pinned by TestPhaseNATRodata_TheImagesAgree, which FAILS if it closes.

The STRING stage is reserved PROGRAM-WIDE by the self-hosted driver, over the oracle's FIVE operations (concat, string equality, string slicing, push and a string field assignment -- pkg/native/program.go:4454), and the frames now match the oracle's exactly. ONE difference remains, and it is the ORACLE's over-approximation rather than the driver's: the oracle's string inference is NAME-based and program-wide, so a name bound to a string ANYWHERE in the program makes that name a string EVERYWHERE -- shadowing included -- and the oracle therefore reserves the staging area (and allocates an arena) for a program that performs no string operation. Its own EMISSION disagrees with its scan: the same program runs and prints an integer sum. The driver follows its emission rather than copying the over-approximation. Measured: the oracle reserves 2560 bytes in both frames of such a program, the driver none. Pinned by TestPhaseNATStrStage_TheOracleNameQuirkIsNotReproduced.

The oracle's string-field WRITE stages the (pointer, length) pair through the string staging area and the driver's does not -- it stores the pair directly into the field area. The FRAME matches the oracle's exactly, but the field-assignment IMAGE is 25 bytes SHORTER on the driver (measured: 443 against 468) and its rodata therefore starts at a different file offset. The oracle's staging implementation is not duplicated.

`while`, the C-style `for` and `for ... in` over an ARRAY VARIABLE are lowered; a literal iterator, `break`/`continue` OUTSIDE a loop, and the arena-using constructs inside a loop are refused by name.

The heap arena is sized at compile time on the assumption that each allocation site runs at most once, so a string concatenation, a `push()` or a map insertion inside a loop is refused. No iteration-scoped arena checkpoint exists, because proving that no live reference escapes an iteration is a separate analysis.

`push()` is lowered by `native-ast`, but a `push()` program built through the native CLI target is currently refused by the PE patch guard (`native pe: rodata patch ... does not fit the section body`). The failure is pre-existing and out of scope for the for-in slice; it is pinned by TestPhase151A9I_RefusalsAreByName/push_pe_patch_guard so it cannot be mistaken for a silent success.
A comparison is a CONDITION, not a value: `let c = (a < b)` is refused.
KIR is verified by the compiler on the default check path but is NOT the backend's input. The native driver consumes the AST directly. Wiring KIR into the backend is not done.
